clinicalPearls: Pathological overgrowth of normal, unencapsulated fat in the epidural space that can compress the thecal sac and nerve roots
Strongly associated with exogenous corticosteroid excess (long-term steroid therapy or Cushing syndrome) and with obesity
Most often affects the thoracic and lumbar spine
Presentations include back pain, radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication, and, in severe thoracic disease, myelopathy
MRI is diagnostic, showing abundant high-T1-signal epidural fat compressing the sac, classically in a stellate or Y-shaped pattern in the lumbar region
Identifying and reversing the underlying cause is central to management
First-line treatment is conservative, with weight reduction and tapering or stopping exogenous corticosteroids where possible
Surgical decompression with debulking of epidural fat is reserved for severe neurological compromise or failure of conservative measures
reference.pathophysiology: Spinal epidural lipomatosis is the abnormal accumulation of histologically normal adipose tissue within the epidural space. It is most commonly driven by states of corticosteroid excess, whether from prolonged exogenous steroid use or endogenous Cushing syndrome, and by obesity, although idiopathic cases are also described. The excess fat encroaches on the limited epidural space and compresses the thecal sac and its neural contents. In the lumbar region the compressed sac takes on a characteristic stellate or Y-shaped configuration, whereas thoracic disease can compress the cord and cause myelopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar spinal stenosis from disc, facet, and ligamentum changes
Angiolipoma or other epidural fatty tumour
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spine as the diagnostic test, showing excess high-T1-signal epidural fat compressing the sac
CT demonstrating low-attenuation epidural fat when MRI is unavailable
Review of corticosteroid exposure and assessment for Cushing syndrome
Metabolic and endocrine work-up, including for hypercortisolism, where clinically indicated
Assessment of body-mass index and obesity-related comorbidities
redFlags: Progressive myelopathy or cauda equina features such as saddle anaesthesia and sphincter dysfunction
Severe canal compromise on imaging with neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Symptoms often stabilise or improve when the underlying cause is addressed, notably with weight loss and reduction of corticosteroids; severe or myelopathic cases may need surgery, after which outcomes depend on the degree and duration of pre-operative compression.
pitfalls: Failing to review and reduce exogenous corticosteroids as the treatable driver
Attributing canal compromise solely to degenerative stenosis and missing the excess epidural fat
references: Fogel et al: Spinal epidural lipomatosis review, The Spine Journal
management: Identify and reverse the underlying cause by tapering exogenous corticosteroids where possible and treating endogenous Cushing syndrome
Institute structured weight loss and management of obesity-related comorbidities as the cornerstone in obese patients
Provide analgesia and physiotherapy for back pain, radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication
Reserve surgical decompression, such as laminectomy with debulking of epidural fat, for severe, progressive or myelopathic disease
Monitor neurological status and repeat MRI to track the epidural fat burden and response to cause-directed treatment
Refer to endocrinology for hypercortisolism assessment and to spinal surgery for compressive or myelopathic presentations
